claim: Animal genomes are organized into topologically associated domains (TADs).
source: Animal genomes are organized into topologically associated domains (TADs).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: TADs are thought to contribute to gene regulation by facilitating enhancer-promoter (E-P) contacts within a TAD and preventing these contacts across TAD borders.
source: TADs are thought to contribute to gene regulation by facilitating enhancer-promoter (E-P) contacts within a TAD and preventing these contacts across TAD borders.
evidence: This represents the prevailing hypothesis in the field about TAD function.

claim: The absolute difference in contact frequency across TAD boundaries is usually less than 2-fold.
source: However, the absolute difference in contact frequency across TAD boundaries is usually less than 2-fold, even though disruptions of TAD borders can change gene expression by 10-fold.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Disruptions of TAD borders can change gene expression by 10-fold.
source: However, the absolute difference in contact frequency across TAD boundaries is usually less than 2-fold, even though disruptions of TAD borders can change gene expression by 10-fold.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Existing models fail to explain the hypersensitive response of gene expression to small changes in contact frequency.
source: Existing models fail to explain this hypersensitive response.
evidence: This is the motivation for the authors' work, based on their analysis of existing literature.

claim: A futile cycle model of enhancer-mediated regulation can exhibit hypersensitivity through bistability and hysteresis.
source: Here, we propose a futile cycle model of enhancer-mediated regulation that can exhibit hypersensitivity through bistability and hysteresis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and stochastic simulations presented in Figures 3-5.

claim: The futile cycle model does not exhibit strong correlation between E-P contact and promoter activity, even though regulation occurs through contact.
source: Consistent with recent experiments, this regulation does not exhibit strong correlation between E-P contact and promoter activity, even though regulation occurs through contact.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 through simulations and comparison with experimental data.

claim: TADs are defined as contiguous regions of the genome where intra-region 3D proximity is greater than inter-region.
source: The genomes of many organisms have been shown to adopt a domain-like structure commonly referred to as topologically associated domains (TADs) (Ibrahim and Mundlos, 2020; Jerković et al., 2020; McCord et al., 2020; Rowley and Corces, 2018), defined as contiguous regions of the genome where intra-region 3D proximity is greater than inter-region (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is the standard definition of TADs in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: TADs can be detected by a range of distinct techniques, including methods relying on proximity ligation like 3C/Hi-C.
source: They can be detected by a range of distinct techniques, including methods relying on proximity ligation like 3C/Hi-C (Jerković et al., 2020; Kempfer and Pombo, 2020; McCord et al., 2020; Rowley and Corces, 2018), ligation-free sequencing methods like GAM (Beagrie et al., 2017) and SPRITE (Quinodoz et al., 2018), microscopy methods such as ORCA (Bintu et al., 2018; Mateo et al., 2019), and even live-cell measurements like DAMC (Redolfi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to different experimental methods.

claim: TADs are a statistical property that emerges from a population of cells dynamically exploring multiple conformational states, rather than a static structure found in all cells.
source: Recent microscopy experiments have shown that TADs are a statistical property that emerges from a population of cells dynamically exploring multiple conformational states, rather than a static structure found in all cells (Bintu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to microscopy experiments.

claim: Many TAD boundaries demarcate regions of co-expressed genes and separate differentially expressed genes.
source: For example, many TAD boundaries demarcate regions of co-expressed genes and separate differentially expressed genes, suggesting that they play a role in cis-regulatory specificity (Long et al., 2016; McCord et al., 2020; Spielmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing this pattern.

claim: Inter-TAD contacts often reach only half the frequency of intra-TAD contacts.
source: Opposing this interpretation, it has been noted that the quantitative difference in interaction frequency is generally small: inter-TAD contacts often reach only half the frequency of intra-TAD contacts, raising questions of how such small differences could explain such clear separation of expression (McCord et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Disruption of TAD boundaries by cis-mutation has been proposed as the causal driver of substantial alterations in gene expression for a variety of disease conditions.
source: The disruption of TAD boundaries by cis-mutation has been proposed as the causal driver of the substantial alterations in gene expression for a variety of disease conditions, a conclusion supported by animal models (Dowen et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2016; Lupiáñez et al., 2015) reviewed in Long et al., 2016; McCord et al., 2020; Spielmann et al., 2018.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to animal model studies and reviews.

claim: Global disruption of TAD boundaries by depletion of boundary-associated factors led to few substantial changes in gene expression in cell culture models.
source: However, global disruption of TAD boundaries by depletion of boundary-associated factors led to few substantial changes in gene expression in cell culture models (Cuartero et al., 2018; Nora et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Stik et al., 2020; Zuin et al., 2014), though such depletion does obstruct the ability of macrophages to respond to inflammatory stimuli (Cuartero et al., 2018; Stik et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Genetic experiments have made it clear that enhancers act on promoters only in cis, suggesting a requirement for physical proximity.
source: Genetic experiments have made it clear that enhancers act on promoters only in cis, suggesting a requirement for physical proximity that would explain the functional role of TADs (Furlong and Levine, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of genetic experiments.

claim: Recent microscopy experiments uncovered little correlation between enhancer-promoter proximity and nascent transcription activity at well-studied loci.
source: However, recent microscopy experiments uncovered little correlation between enhancer-promoter (E-P) proximity and nascent transcription activity at well-studied loci (Alexander et al., 2019; Mateo et al., 2019) reviewed in Finn and Misteli, 2019b.
evidence: This is supported by citations to microscopy studies and a review.

claim: Deletion of a few kilobases of sequence at the border of the Ubx and abd-A TADs resulted in a 1-2.5-fold increase in interaction frequency between the domains.
source: Deletion of only a few kilobases of sequence at the border of these TADs resulted in a clear increase in interaction between the domains, including between Ubx enhancers and the abd-A promoter. However, interaction frequency increased only by a factor of 1–2.5-fold across the population (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is quantified from published data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TAD border deletion at the Ubx/abd-A locus resulted in a fivefold increase in mRNA counts of abd-A.
source: The change in gene expression, as assayed by single-molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH), was hypersensitive to this moderate change in contact frequency, with an average fivefold increase in mRNA counts of abd-A (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is quantified from published data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In wildtype cells, 25% of individual cells showed some cross-TAD border mixing between the Ubx enhancers and the abd-A promoter compared to 50% of mutant cells.
source: Moreover, while the structures were easily distinguished at the population level, the structures of single cells were more variable (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), with 25% of individual wildtype cells showing some cross-TAD border mixing between the Ubx enhancers and the abd-A promoter compared to 50% of mutant cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is quantified from published data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The quantitative disconnect between weak TAD borders and large transcriptional effects of border disruption is not an artifact of Hi-C or of population averaging.
source: From these single-cell analyses, we concluded that the quantitative disconnect between weak TAD borders (see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and the large transcriptional effects of border disruption (see also Figure 1—figure supplement 4) is not an artifact of Hi-C or of population averaging.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the authors' analysis of single-cell data shown in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Small differences in the frequency of contact appear sufficient to drive large changes in expression.
source: Instead, small differences in the frequency of contact appear sufficient to drive large changes in expression, requiring us to re-examine the textbook picture of E-P regulation (Alberts et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: A two-state enhancer model with one TF-binding site exhibits only sublinear responses to TF concentration.
source: From this result, we see, for any value kon or koff, the probability that the enhancer is bound (and therefore whether it can activate transcription) exhibits only sublinear responses to A (i.e., is never hypersensitive) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A three-state enhancer model with two identical binding sites can be hypersensitive to TF concentration when koff2/kon2 < koff1/kon1.
source: From this equation, we observe that for the special case where koff2/kon2 < koff1/kon1, this system is hypersensitive to A (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The enhancer cooperativity model is rejected because it does not match observed data on contact frequency changes.
source: Unfortunately, this model is immediately rejected by available data. Upon perturbation of TAD boundaries, we (Figure 1A) and others do not observe the appearance or loss of cooperative enhancer contacts of great enough magnitude to explain the change in transcription (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The GTF condensate model can achieve a hypersensitive regime where small fold changes in E-P contact lead to large fold changes in transcription.
source: This simple model version includes a regime in which condensate size (a proxy for transcription) is hypersensitive to changes in 3D structure, as illustrated by simulations of the Markov jump process (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through stochastic simulations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Hypersensitive behavior in the GTF condensate model requires cluster size greater than 2.
source: We saw that sensitivity increased with cluster size, and hypersensitive behavior required cluster size greater than 2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown through parameter sweeps in Figure 3E.

claim: Recent experimental work supports the formation of condensates of GTFs such as PolII, Mediator, and BRD4 at promoters.
source: Recent experimental work supports the formation of condensates of GTFs such as PolII, Mediator, and BRD4 at the promoters, (Chong et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2018), and provides experimental evidence for enhanced capture/reduced release (Chong et al., 2018) as expected for phase separating condensates.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The PTM futile cycle model can achieve a hypersensitive regime in which small fold changes in E-P contact lead to large fold changes in transcription.
source: The PTM futile cycle model version can also achieve a hypersensitive regime in which small fold changes in E-P contact lead to large fold changes in transcription (Figure 3J), around the experimentally observed range (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through stochastic simulations shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Two promoters differing by a factor of 2 in condensate dissolution or tag removal rate can respond differently to the same change in E-P interaction frequency.
source: For both versions of the model, Promoter 1 exhibited a large (greater than twofold) increase in transcription, yet Promoter 2 remained almost unaffected in response to the twofold perturbation of the E-P interaction frequency (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The apparent specificity of E-P interactions may be an illusion resulting from different tipping points among promoters.
source: These simulations illustrate that the apparent specificity ('lock and key') may be an illusion resulting from different tipping points among promoters, which arise from regulating accumulation/depletion of TF condensates or promoter-associated PTMs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both the condensate and PTM model versions readily exhibit hysteresis.
source: We found that, in addition to exhibiting hypersensitivity, both the condensate and PTM model versions readily exhibited hysteresis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: The futile cycle models exhibit qualitatively distinct sensitivities of transcription rate to small changes in E-P interaction at short time scales compared to long time scales.
source: Because of the hysteresis in the system, we observed qualitatively distinct sensitivities of the average transcription rate to small changes in E-P interaction at short time scales than we saw at long time scales (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both the condensate and PTM simulations exhibited a weak (less than twofold) change in transcription in most simulated cells by the early time point.
source: Both the condensate and the PTM simulations exhibited a weak (less than twofold) change in transcription in most of the simulated cells of the population by the early time point, even though this was sufficient for enhancer deactivation to lead most of the population to drop into the low expressing state (Figure 5F, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 5F, G.

claim: The odds ratios for observing transcription given E-P contact in the simulations were statistically greater than 1, but only by a small margin of 0-30%.
source: Across the different regimes of E-P contact frequency, the odds ratios were statistically greater than 1, but only by a small margin of 0–30%, paralleling our recent empirical observation (Mateo et al., 2019; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 6B, C and comparison with experimental data in Figure 6D.

claim: Contact-dependent mechanisms of E-P regulation can be consistent with empirical data in which many transcribing cells lack contacts and vice versa.
source: These simulations demonstrate that contact-dependent mechanisms of E-P regulation can be still consistent with empirical data in which many transcribing cells lack contacts and vice versa.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: For a moderate number of simulated bursts (~500), no detectable increase in E-P proximity was found at any time scales relative to transcription bursts.
source: For a moderate number of simulated bursts (~500), we also found no detectable increase in proximity at any time scales relative to that of the burst (Figure 6F, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 6F, G.

claim: Substantially increasing the number of simulated cells (~20,000) uncovered weak but statistically significant correlations between E-P contact and transcription.
source: Substantially increasing the number of simulated cells (~20,000) uncovered weak but statistically significant correlations in each of these cases (Figure 6H, I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, F), similar to the observations from the Drosophila data (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 6H, I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, F.

claim: Enhancers could regulate genes like Sox2 or the Bithorax genes in a purely contact-dependent manner, even without strong correlation between contact events and transcription at the single-cell level.
source: Thus, these models show that enhancers could regulate genes like Sox2 or the Bithorax genes in a purely contact-dependent manner, even without strong correlation between contact events and transcription at the single-cell level.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The futile cycle model provides an explanation for why TAD boundaries can be weak and yet be major regulators of transcription.
source: These include (1) why TAD boundaries can be weak and why insulators only mildly affect contact frequency and yet be major regulators of transcription
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their modeling results.

claim: The futile cycle model explains why many genes thought to be responsive to distal enhancers are insensitive to some structural changes.
source: (2) why many genes thought to be responsive to distal enhancers are insensitive to some structural changes
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The futile cycle model explains why global disruption of structure and acute disruption of structure have been reported to have distinct effects on transcription.
source: (3) why global disruption of structure and acute disruption of structure have been reported to have distinct effects on transcription
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The futile cycle model explains why physical distance between known distal enhancers and their cognate gene does not show obvious correlation with transcriptional state in single cells.
source: (4) why physical distance between known distal enhancers and their cognate gene does not show obvious correlation with transcriptional state in single cells.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: A futile cycle promoter exhibits not just hypersensitive response to contact interactions, but also substantial regimes of sublinear or insensitive response.
source: A futile cycle promoter exhibits not just hypersensitive response to contact interactions, but also substantial regimes of sublinear or insensitive response.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Promoter-specific differences in the intrinsic addition or removal of tags can render one promoter unresponsive to an enhancer that activates a second promoter, even though the two experience similar absolute interaction frequency.
source: Promoter-specific differences in the intrinsic addition or removal of tags (or the recruitment of GTFs to a promoter condensate) can render one promoter unresponsive to an enhancer that activates a second promoter, even though the two experience similar absolute interaction frequency.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transgene assays indicate most regulatory elements will promiscuously activate most promoters if placed close enough.
source: This is notable since transgene assays indicate most regulatory elements will promiscuously activate most promoters if placed close enough (Arnold et al., 2013; Furlong and Levine, 2018; Kvon, 2015; Kvon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to transgene assay studies.

claim: Decreasing E-P contact frequency by increasing E-P distance within a TAD produced a sharp drop in expression in Drosophila enhancers.
source: Such an experiment has recently been published with Drosophila enhancers, and results are consistent with the model prediction—decreasing E-P contact frequency by increasing E-P distance within a TAD produced a sharp drop in expression (Yokoshi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Manipulations of the Sox9 locus that progressively increased contact frequency between Sox9 enhancers and the adjacent Kcnj2 gene exhibited a nonlinear response.
source: Similarly, manipulations of the Sox9 locus, which progressively increased the contact frequency between Sox9 enhancers and the adjacent Kcnj2 gene by deleting first the TAD border between them and then further shortening the distance, also exhibited just such a nonlinear response (Despang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Systematic variation of the distance between the Sox2 promoter and one of its enhancers reveals a strikingly hypersensitive dependence of transcription on E-P contact frequency.
source: Most notably, systematic variation of the distance between the Sox2 promoter and one of its enhancers, both inserted into an ectopic site, reveals a strikingly hypersensitive dependence of transcription on E-P contact frequency (Zuin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Transcription was assayed only hours after contact changes in the cohesin degron experiment.
source: Transcription was assayed only hours after the contact changes in the degron experiment, which may explain why little change was detected.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on the timing of the experiments.

claim: Experiments that genetically deleted border elements assayed transcription days and many cell generations later.
source: In contrast, experiments that genetically deleted border elements assayed transcription days and many cell generations later, at which point some promoters saw major changes in expression.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on the timing of the experiments.

claim: Transcriptional assays performed at longer intervals after first detection of E-P contact disruption exhibit greater transcriptional changes.
source: Yet, by and large, transcriptional assays performed at longer intervals after first detection of E-P contact disruption exhibit greater transcriptional changes, consistent with the explanation suggested by these simulations.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on comparison of different experimental studies.

claim: Studies reporting condensates of GTFs such as Med1, PolII, and Brd4 indicate a stability that generally exceeds the imaging time.
source: Nonetheless, studies reporting condensates of GTFs such as Med1, PolII, and Brd4 indicate a stability that generally exceeds the imaging time (Chong et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: It has been widely expected that active promoters should colocalize with their active enhancers, based largely on bulk population assays.
source: It has been widely expected that active promoters should colocalize with their active enhancers, based largely on bulk population assays such 3C and H3K27ac Hi-ChIP (Bartman et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2012; Kagey et al., 2010; Mumbach et al., 2017, Mumbach et al., 2016; Rao et al., 2014; Williamson et al., 2016); for review see Furlong and Levine, 2018.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies and a review.

claim: Recent single-cell measurements found that cells with close E-P proximity were only slightly more likely to exhibit nascent transcription than those lacking contact.
source: Surprisingly, recent single-cell measurements found that cells with close E-P proximity were only slightly more likely to exhibit nascent transcription than those lacking contact (Finn and Misteli, 2019b; Mateo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to single-cell measurement studies.

claim: Live-cell tagging of chromatin proximal to the enhancer and promoter of Sox2 coupled with live-cell measurements of nascent RNA transcription uncovered no significant correlation between E-P proximity and transcription activity.
source: However, recent live-cell imaging experiments suggest otherwise: live-cell tagging of chromatin proximal to the enhancer and promoter of Sox2 coupled with live-cell measurements of nascent RNA transcription uncovered no significant correlation between E-P proximity and transcription activity (Alexander et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a live-cell imaging study.

claim: The futile cycle model demonstrates that it is possible for transcription to be regulated by E-P contact and yet show little temporal correlation, even in live, single-cell time-lapse data.
source: The futile cycle model demonstrates that it is possible for transcription to be regulated by E-P contact and yet show little temporal correlation, even in live, single-cell time-lapse data.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Individual E-P contact events have little impact on promoter state, contributing to only marginally more promoter tags or larger condensates.
source: This is because individual E-P contact events have little impact on promoter state, contributing to only marginally more promoter tags or larger condensates.
evidence: This is inferred from the model structure and simulation results.

claim: With sufficient observations, a weak correlation between E-P contact and transcription should be detectable.
source: This explanation can be directly tested with larger data sets—with sufficient observations, a weak correlation should be detectable (as seen in the fixed cell data), since cells experiencing a higher frequency of contact are more likely to have a high level of tag and thus more likely to transcribe, even though it is not a one-to-one dependency.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: It is equally plausible that futile cycles of repressive condensates or tags at the promoter account for hypersensitivity of some promoters.
source: However, it is equally plausible that futile cycles of repressive condensates or tags at the promoter account for hypersensitivity of some promoters.
evidence: This is a speculation by the authors about alternative implementations of the model.

claim: Through accumulation of local tags or GTFs in a condensate, the promoter is able to integrate its history of interaction with one or more regulatory elements and respond in striking nonlinear ways to changes in these signals.
source: Instead, through accumulation of local tags or GTFs in a condensate, the promoter is able to integrate its history of interaction with one or more regulatory elements and respond in striking nonlinear ways to changes in these signals.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their modeling results.
